title: Deterministic extension load order, and collision resolution made explicit
wave: M2 wave 2 (shippable; WI-2 splits into 2 PRs — the sort is a real behavior change and goes alone, the diagnostic rides along)
one_line: Extensions are now always loaded in sorted path order instead of whatever order the filesystem happened to hand back, and when two extensions register the same tool name the winner is both a documented rule and a diagnostic that names both sides.
user_visible_effect: Two plugins that register the same tool name resolve to the same one on every machine, every run, and after every reinstall — instead of silently flipping with directory layout. The losing registration is also reported by name and path, so 'my extension never registered' finally has a signal instead of silence. A user who listed extensions in a specific order in settings and relied on that order winning will see the order become alphabetical; that is the intended flip and is called out in the changelog.

steps.instruction: In loader.ts, insert a comment block plus `allPaths.sort((a, b) => (a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0));` on the line immediately before `return allPaths;`. The comment must say: (a) why — registration is last-extension-wins, so a filesystem-dependent order is a silent user-visible behavior change; (b) that this is a code-unit comparator, not localeCompare, so the winner does not depend on host locale; (c) that it sits after dedup and after every discovery branch so all four contribute to one order. Do NOT touch `addPath`/`addPaths` — they are the dedup and disable-filter layer and are correct as-is.

In helpers.ts, replace the single `const entries = await readDirEntries(dir);` line with a statement that first awaits readDirEntries, spreads the result into a new array, and sorts that copy by `entry.name` with a code-unit comparator. The comment MUST state that readDirEntries returns the module-level dirCache array by reference and that sorting in place would reorder the cache for the six other discovery modules — this is the single easiest mistake to make here and it is silent. Also state that a post-sort in discoverExtensionPaths cannot repair this function, because the Promise.all below pushes from inside its callbacks so the result order is I/O-completion order.

In types.ts, add `export interface ExtensionRegistrationDiagnostic` right after the RegisteredTool interface closes. Four fields: `type: string` (documented as staying `"warning"` for both current producers, present so a future producer can be filtered), `message: string` (documented as required to name EVERY conflicting side so a log-only consumer sees both), `path: string` (the last-wins winner, or the single side when there is no conflict), and `paths: string[]` (every conflicting side in load order, last entry is the winner).

In runner.ts, add the private `#collectToolNameCollisions(): ExtensionRegistrationDiagnostic[]` method. Walk `this.extensions` in order, build a Map<toolName, string[]> of registrant paths, then emit one diagnostic per name with two or more registrants. Use the LAST path as both `path` and the message's stated winner. The message must contain every path as text. Return the array. Note in a comment that Map insertion order makes the diagnostic list itself deterministic once load order is.

In runner.ts, retype the private field as `#registrationDiagnostics: ExtensionRegistrationDiagnostic[] = []` and rename all four references (declaration, reset, push, return). At the end of `getRegisteredCommands`, after the command loop and before the return, push `...this.#collectToolNameCollisions()`. Deliberately do NOT add a `logger.warn` for tool collisions — the reserved-command path at 1193-1196 logs only when `!this.hasUI()`, and a plugin tree can produce many collisions; recording them without logging keeps startup quiet while still surfacing them to any consumer that reads the report.

In runner.ts, widen `getCommandDiagnostics()` to return `ExtensionRegistrationDiagnostic[]` (the array element type changes, the method name and the `path` field do not). Add `getToolCollisionDiagnostics(): ExtensionRegistrationDiagnostic[]` that returns `this.#collectToolNameCollisions()` computed fresh. Keep the doc comment on both explaining that `#registrationDiagnostics` is only populated once `getRegisteredCommands()` has run, which is exactly why the tool getter recomputes rather than filtering. Add the top-level import of `ExtensionRegistrationDiagnostic` from `./types` to the existing type import block — top-level only, no inline import.

In runner.ts, expand the one-line doc comment above `getRegisteredTool` into the rule statement: extensions bind in `discoverExtensionPaths` order, which is sorted by path; on a duplicate tool name the registration from the extension whose path sorts LAST wins; the shadowed registration is still returned by `getAllRegisteredTools()`; and the collision is reported by `#collectToolNameCollisions` / `getToolCollisionDiagnostics`. This is the sentence WI-2 exists to write down — the reverse-walk loop body itself does not change.

Write the new test file. Structure: `TempDir.createSync("@omp-ext-order-")` in beforeEach, `removeSync()` in afterEach. Build a fixture directory `<temp>/exts/` containing 8 subdirectories `ext-a` .. `ext-h`, each with an `index.ts` registering a tool named `dup` with a distinct label. The fixture dir MUST contain no `package.json` and no `index.ts`/`index.js` directly — a direct index short-circuits `resolveExtensionDirectory` to a single file at directory-resolution.ts:109-110 and the test becomes vacuous, and a package.json makes the manifest branch authoritative at 106-107.

Add the fixture-premise check inside the test, before the subprocess runs: call `fs.readdirSync(extsDir)` and assert its order is NOT already sorted. This is the check the plan called for, with one correction — it must use `fs.readdirSync`, NOT `readDirEntries`, because the configured-directory branch of `discoverExtensionPaths` goes through `resolveExtensionDirectory`, which uses raw `fs.readdirSync` at directory-resolution.ts:114 and never touches the cached capability helper. Checking with the wrong primitive would validate a premise about a code path the fixture does not exercise. On failure, throw an error whose message names the actual order and instructs the engineer to rename the subdirectories until readdir returns them out of lexical order — never a silent skip.

Add the row-1 probe. Add the changelog entries under `## [Unreleased]`, one line under `### Changed`. test_contract:
Two externally observable contracts, each with a named failure mode.

ROW 1 — "Extension load order is sorted, so a duplicate tool name always resolves to the lexicographically-last registrant, across fresh processes." Observable: `ExtensionRunner#getRegisteredTool("dup")?.extensionPath`. If this regresses, a user with two installed plugins registering the same tool name gets whichever one readdir happened to yield first — so the same install resolves differently on APFS vs ext4, before vs after a reinstall that changes directory layout, and the flip is silent (no log, no error, the losing plugin just appears not to exist). Why the winner's NAME and not a cross-run consistency assertion: raw readdir order is a property of the DIRECTORY, not the process, so two subprocesses reading the same fixture directory see the same order with or without a sort. A consistency-only assertion passes identically on an implementation that sorts nothing, which is why the fixture is built to make readdir order differ from lexical order and the premise is verified in-test with fs.readdirSync before the subprocess runs. Why two subprocesses rather than two in-process calls: the module-level dirCache (capability/fs.ts:5) and Bun's ESM module cache both survive a second call and would mask the very ordering under test. This row FAILS on HEAD and passes only after the loader.ts sort.

ROW 2 — "A duplicate tool name is reported as a diagnostic naming both registering sides." Observable: `ExtensionRunner#getToolCollisionDiagnostics()` returns a record whose `paths` holds exactly the two registrants and whose `message` contains both path strings. If this regresses, a plugin author whose tool is silently overridden by another plugin has no signal at all — the override is invisible in the UI, the logs, and the API, and the only symptom is a tool that behaves differently than its source says. `message` is asserted to carry both paths as text so the log-only consumer path is defended, not just the structured field.

What is deliberately NOT asserted: that the `allPaths` array is sorted. That is internal array shape; the winner's identity is the contract, and asserting the array would let an implementer satisfy the test by sorting in the wrong layer.

gate:
Four-part, and every part is able to go red.

(1) TYPE: `bun run check:ts` exits 0. Goes red if the diagnostic interface is exported wrong, the top-level type import is missing, or an `any` leaks in.

(2) ROW 1 DISCRIMINATES: with the fix reverted, row 1 reports a winner that is NOT `ext-h`. This is only a real gate because the test first proves its own fixture premise — it reads the fixture directory with `fs.readdirSync` (the same primitive `resolveExtensionDirectory` uses at directory-resolution.ts:114) and refuses to proceed if readdir already happens to return lexical order, in which case the assertion would be vacuous and would pass on an implementation that sorts nothing.

(3) ROW 2 DISCRIMINATES: with `#collectToolNameCollisions` removed, row 2 gets zero diagnostics and goes red on `paths` and on the message substring check.

(4) NO REGRESSION: `bun test test/extensions-discovery.test.ts` stays green, and `test/extension-loader-concurrency.test.ts` stays green — that file is the standing guard that `loadExtensions` imports concurrently while binding factories in path order, and the loader sort must not disturb it.
blocks: WI-7 (wave 5 registerMode) — hard prerequisite. The mode registry creates order-sensitive registrations of its own, so it must land on top of a defined order, not on filesystem order.
WI-6 (wave 4) — the wave table states WI-6 needs WI-2's collision rule settled before it can safely change priority ordering.
effort: S. Two sorts, one private collector, one exported interface, one doc paragraph, one new test file, one changelog line. The sort half is well under an hour; the test is the bulk of it because the fixture has to be built so that it actually discriminates.
risk: MEDIUM, and it is a real behavior change rather than a defect fix — that is the whole reason the plan splits this into two PRs. A user with two same-named plugins today is relying on an accidental order, and the fix flips it. The second, quieter risk is the in-place sort: `readDirEntries` returns the cached `fs.Dirent[]` by reference, so `[...entries].sort()` written as `entries.sort()` mutates a module-level cache shared by six other discovery modules and silently reorders their results too. That produces no error and no failing import — it is the failure mode most likely to reach main, and the comment at helpers.ts:763 is the only thing standing between a tired engineer and it.
open_questions: Does the post-sort apply to EXPLICITLY configured paths too? Sorting `allPaths` wholesale (the plan's choice, and what step 1 implements) means a user who writes `extensions: ["b-ext", "a-ext"]` in settings and relies on b-ext winning now gets a-ext. Sorting only the ambient/discovered entries and preserving configured order would honor intent better but makes the rule harder to state and the test fixture would have to use the ambient path. The plan settled on wholesale; this needs a human to confirm before the PR is opened, because it is the one part of WI-2 a user could reasonably call a regression.

Should the 8-extension fixture's degenerate-premise check hard-fail or skip? Hard-failing is honest and is what the plan chose, but on a filesystem whose readdir happens to return lexical order the row goes red on a platform that is not broken. Skipping silently reintroduces the exact vacuous pass the plan was written to prevent. A third option — assert the winner name unconditionally and record the premise in the failure text only — trades a rare red for a permanently weaker test on some platforms. Pick one before writing the test.

The linked-module sort at helpers.ts:763 has no observable coverage in this WI's fixture, because the fixture exercises the configured-directory path (which the loader post-sort already fixes). Gate step (3) above proves the two sorts are not redundant but cannot prove the helpers.ts sort does anything. Options: build a second fixture that forces `discoverExtensionModulePaths`'s linked-directory branch (symlinked subdirectory containing index.ts, which native glob does not descend into), or accept that the helpers.ts sort rests on a code-reading argument and say so in the PR. This needs a human decision because the second fixture is most of the remaining test effort.

Does `getCommandDiagnostics()` have out-of-repo consumers (published SDK, downstream forks)? `git grep -rn "getCommandDiagnostics" -- packages/` matches only the definition at runner.ts:1206, so nothing IN this repo needs updating — but widening its element type is still a published-API surface change. Confirm the SDK's public exports before widening rather than relying on the in-repo grep alone.
